I represent about fifteen artists, and part of my job is helping them say no. Artists are often terrible at it. Either they say yes to everything and overcommit, or they disappear and never answer the email. Both are worse than a clear refusal. A good no has three parts. First, thank the person, because somebody chose you, and that matters. Second, give the real reason in one sentence. Not five excuses. One reason. And third, make a counter-proposal. Offer an older work, a later date, a smaller version. The curator who hears, I'm afraid I can't, but would it work if I sent you this instead, does not feel rejected. She feels that she is still working with you. The artists who do this well are the ones I see invited again, year after year. A gracious no is not the end of a relationship. Very often, it is the beginning.

I run an arts program in a large public hospital, and every year I invite about thirty artists to work with us. Around half of them say no, and that is fine. What I remember is how they say it. One painter wrote back the same day. She was flattered, she had a prior commitment until March, and she asked if we could talk again in the spring. We did, and she has worked with us for four years now. Another artist said yes, came twice, and then stopped answering our emails. That was much harder for our patients than a refusal would have been. So my advice is simple. If you do not have the bandwidth, say so early. If some part of the request is non-negotiable for you, the fee, the schedule, the consent forms, say that too. I would rather hear an honest no in April than a broken yes in June.
